C# fully implements Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, and Polymorphism to model real-world domains.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Encapsulation: Restricting access to internal structures using keywords like private and internal.
  • Inheritance: Reusing class structures via class base inheritance (:).
  • Polymorphism: Declaring virtual methods in base classes and overriding them in subclasses.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public class Animal {
    public virtual void MakeSound() => Console.WriteLine("Generic Sound");
}
public class Cat : Animal {
    public override void MakeSound() => Console.WriteLine("Meow");
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Deep inheritance chains that violate Liskov Substitution, coupling child classes tightly to base class implementations.

questions.question: What is polymorphic method overriding?
questions.answer: Method overriding allows a derived class to provide a specific implementation of a virtual or abstract method defined in a base class.

questions.question: How is abstraction implemented in C#?
questions.answer: Through abstract classes and interface declarations, defining structural contracts without forcing implementation detail.

topics.title: Interfaces & Abstract Classes
topics.html:
Interfaces & Abstract Classes

Course: C# Programming

Interfaces define contracts that classes must implement. Abstract classes are partial implementations that cannot be instantiated on their own.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Interfaces: Contracts declaring methods and properties. Classes can implement multiple interfaces.
  • Abstract Classes: Base classes that can contain implemented methods, backing fields, and state.
  • Default Interface Implementations: C# 8+ feature allowing interfaces to define default method blocks.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public interface ILogger { void Log(string msg); }
public abstract class BaseService {
    public abstract void Process();
    public void LogStart() => Console.WriteLine("Processing start...");
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Adding new methods to public interfaces without default implementations, which breaks all classes implementing that interface in external libraries.

questions.question: Can a class inherit from multiple abstract classes?
questions.answer: No, C# supports single class inheritance. However, a class can implement multiple interfaces.

questions.question: What is the main difference between abstract class and interface?
questions.answer: Abstract classes can hold state (backing fields) and constructors, whereas interfaces cannot hold instance fields and primarily define behavior contracts.

topics.title: Generics & Collections
topics.html:
Generics & Collections

Course: C# Programming

Generics allow classes, methods, and interfaces to be defined with placeholder types, improving code reuse, type safety, and runtime performance.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Generic Constraints: Limiting types with keywords (where T : class, where T : new()).
  • Generic Collections: Types like List and Dictionary.
  • Performance: Avoiding boxing/unboxing overhead when working with value types.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public class Repository<T> where T : class {
    private List<T> items = new List<T>();
    public void Add(T item) => items.Add(item);
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Overusing generic type parameters without constraints, making the inside code compile-errors because the compiler doesn't know what actions the type supports.

questions.question: Why are generic collections preferred over non-generic ones?
questions.answer: They provide compile-time type safety and eliminate boxing/unboxing performance overhead for value types.

questions.question: What does the constraint where T : new() mean?
questions.answer: It specifies that the generic type parameter T must have a public parameterless constructor, allowing instantiation (new T()) inside the class.

topics.title: Exception Handling
topics.html:
Exception Handling

Course: C# Programming

Exception handling intercepts runtime anomalies using try, catch, finally, and custom exception types.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Try-Catch blocks: Surrounding fragile actions and catching specific exceptions (e.g. SqlException).
  • Finally block: Ensuring execution occurs (like closing connections) regardless of exceptions.
  • Throw expressions: Throwing custom exceptions inline.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
try {
    int zero = 0; int x = 10 / zero;
} catch (DivideByZeroException ex) {
    Console.WriteLine($"Error caught: {ex.Message}");
} finally {
    Console.WriteLine("Cleanup completed.");
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Catching the base System.Exception and swallowing it, or rethrowing with "throw ex;" which wipes out the original stack trace instead of using "throw;".

questions.question: What is the difference between "throw ex" and "throw"?
questions.answer: "throw ex" resets the stack trace to the current catch block, losing history. "throw" preserves the entire original stack trace.

questions.question: When should a custom exception be created?
questions.answer: Create custom exceptions when handling domain-specific errors that require custom data or actions not described by system exceptions.

topics.title: Delegates, Events & Lambdas
topics.html:
Delegates, Events & Lambdas

Course: C# Programming

Delegates are type-safe function pointers. Events implement a publish-subscribe model, and Lambdas provide clean, inline anonymous functions.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Delegates: Declaring signature layouts like Action and Func.
  • Events: Encapsulated delegates that prevent external triggers and support += subscriptions.
  • Lambda Expressions: Syntax (input => expression) representing inline function definitions.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public class Publisher {
    public event Action OnChanged; // Event definition
    public void Notify() => OnChanged?.Invoke();
}

Publisher p = new Publisher();
p.OnChanged += () => Console.WriteLine("Notified!");

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Leaking memory by subscribing to events but never unsubscribing. This prevents the garbage collector from reclaiming the subscribing object.

questions.question: What is a delegate?
questions.answer: A delegate is a reference type that defines a method signature, allowing methods to be passed as arguments.

questions.question: How do you prevent memory leaks when using events?
questions.answer: Ensure you unsubscribe from the event using the -= operator when the subscriber is being disposed.

topics.title: LINQ Basics in C#
topics.html:
LINQ Basics in C#

Course: C# Programming

Language Integrated Query (LINQ) provides a SQL-like interface to query collections, XML, and database frameworks.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Extension Methods: LINQ relies on extending IEnumerable with custom query operations.
  • Query Syntax: Declarative queries (from x in source select x).
  • Method Syntax: Functional queries using lambda expressions (source.Select(x => x)).

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
int[] scores = { 90, 71, 82 };
var highScores = scores.Where(s => s > 80).OrderBy(s => s);
foreach (var s in highScores) Console.WriteLine(s);

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Not understanding deferred execution, leading to queries running repeatedly when iterated in loops.

questions.question: What is the main difference between Query and Method syntax?
questions.answer: Query syntax is structured like SQL. Method syntax uses extension methods and lambdas, supporting more operators.

questions.question: What is the purpose of deferred execution in LINQ?
questions.answer: It evaluates queries only when the data is read (e.g. in a foreach loop), optimizing database load.

topics.title: Asynchronous Programming (async/await)
topics.html:
Asynchronous Programming (async/await)

Course: C# Programming

Asynchronous programming uses async, await, and Task objects to run tasks without blocking the main CPU threads.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Task & Task: Represent ongoing execution models that return data in the future.
  • Await Keyword: Non-blocking wait that releases the current thread until the task is complete.
  • Task.ConfigureAwait: Controlling synchronization contexts for background thread returns.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public async Task<string> DownloadWebPageAsync(string url) {
    using HttpClient client = new HttpClient();
    return await client.GetStringAsync(url); // Non-blocking
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using async void instead of async Task for methods that do not return values (except for event handlers), making exception catching impossible.

questions.question: Why is "async void" discouraged?
questions.answer: Exceptions thrown in async void methods cannot be caught by callers and can crash the application process.

questions.question: What is the difference between Task and ValueTask?
questions.answer: ValueTask is a struct that prevents heap allocation when the async method completes synchronously.

topics.title: File I/O & Serialization
topics.html:
File I/O & Serialization

Course: C# Programming

File I/O accesses local disk volumes, while serialization translates memory objects into data streams like JSON or XML.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Streams: Reading and writing binary or text streams (StreamReader, FileStream).
  • JSON Serialization: Converting C# objects into JSON strings using System.Text.Json.
  • Using Statements: Ensuring file locks and buffers are closed automatically.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
using System.IO;
using System.Text.Json;

var user = new { Name = "Ashutosh" };
string json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(user);
File.WriteAllText("user.json", json);

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Forgetting to close or dispose file streams, which leaves locks on the filesystem and causes subsequent operations to fail.

questions.question: What does the using statement do for streams?
questions.answer: It ensures the Stream calls Dispose(), releasing operating system file locks immediately.

questions.question: Which namespace handles modern C# JSON serialization?
questions.answer: System.Text.Json, which is optimized for high-performance and low-memory operations.

topics.title: Memory Management & GC
topics.html:
Memory Management & GC

Course: C# Programming

The Garbage Collector (GC) manages allocation and reclamation of heap memory for managed code.

💡 Key Concepts

  • GC Generations: Allocations are sorted into Gen 0 (short-lived), Gen 1 (buffer), and Gen 2 (long-lived).
  • IDisposable: Interface declaring Dispose() to release unmanaged objects (files, sockets).
  • Finalizers: Fallback methods (~Class) to clean up resources during garbage collection.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public class DatabaseConnector : IDisposable {
    private SqlConnection conn = new SqlConnection();
    public void Dispose() {
        conn.Dispose(); // Release database socket resource
    }
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Calling GC.Collect() manually in code. This triggers full heap evaluations and degrades runtime performance.

questions.question: How do GC generations optimize memory management?
questions.answer: By collecting Gen 0 frequently (where short-lived objects live), avoiding expensive full-heap Gen 2 scans.

questions.question: When should a class implement IDisposable?
questions.answer: When it holds references to unmanaged resources like files, database connections, or network sockets.

topics.title: Pattern Matching & Switch Expressions
topics.html:
Pattern Matching & Switch Expressions

Course: C# Programming

Inspect type shapes, properties, and values in a single expression using modern pattern matching features.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Type Patterns: Checking types and declaring local references inline (is Customer c).
  • Property Patterns: Filtering inside switch constructs by property matches ({ Age: > 18 }).
  • Switch Expressions: Expression-oriented switch syntax using lambda-like mapping (=>).

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public string GetTicketPrice(User u) => u switch {
    { Role: "Admin" } => "Free",
    { Age: < 12 } => "$5",
    _ => "$10" // Default case
};

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Creating overlapping switch patterns where a general case catches values before a specific case checks them.

questions.question: What is the default case in switch expressions?
questions.answer: The discard operator (_) matches any input that did not match previous cases.

questions.question: What is a property pattern?
questions.answer: It checks if properties of an object match specified conditions, evaluating properties inline.

topics.title: Attributes & Reflection
topics.html:
Attributes & Reflection

Course: C# Programming

Reflection allows code metadata inspection and dynamic invocation of objects at runtime.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Attributes: Adding metadata tags to classes, fields, or parameters ([Serializable]).
  • Type Class: Using typeof() or GetType() to fetch metadata reflection properties.
  • Dynamic Instantiation: Creating instances dynamically using Activator.CreateInstance.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
var type = typeof(string);
var methods = type.GetMethods();
Console.WriteLine($"String class has {methods.Length} methods.");

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using reflection in hot paths (frequently called loops). Reflection lookup is slow and degrades performance.

questions.question: What is Reflection in C#?
questions.answer: Reflection provides metadata descriptions of classes, assemblies, and modules, allowing dynamic object creation.

questions.question: Why is Reflection slower than static calls?
questions.answer: Because it involves runtime metadata table searches, type resolving, and string matching instead of compile-time calls.

topics.title: Multithreading & Parallel Programming
topics.html:
Multithreading & Parallel Programming

Course: C# Programming

Run concurrent CPU operations using Thread, ThreadPool, Task Parallel Library (TPL), and Parallel.ForEach.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Thread vs Task: Threads are operating system constructs. Tasks are managed models representing execution units.
  • Lock & Thread Safety: Preventing race conditions using the lock keyword on private objects.
  • Parallel.ForEach: Splitting loop operations across multiple CPU cores automatically.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
private static object _lock = new object();
private static int _count = 0;

public void Increment() {
    lock (_lock) {
        _count++; // Thread safe
    }
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Deadlocks, which happen when Thread A locks Resource X and waits for Resource Y, while Thread B locks Y and waits for X.

questions.question: What is a deadlock and how do you prevent it?
questions.answer: A deadlock occurs when threads block each other waiting for resources. Prevent it by locking resources in a consistent order and using timeouts.

questions.question: What is the Task Parallel Library (TPL)?
questions.answer: A set of APIs that simplify adding parallelism and concurrency by scheduling tasks across threads.

topics.title: C# Modern Features (C# 10-13)
topics.html:
C# Modern Features (C# 10-13)

Course: C# Programming

Explore new compiler additions including primary constructors, global using statements, file-scoped namespaces, and collection expressions.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Primary Constructors: Declaring constructor parameters inline on class definitions.
  • File-Scoped Namespaces: Reducing bracket nesting by ending namespace declarations with a semicolon.
  • Collection Expressions: Using bracket syntax ([1, 2, 3]) to define collections.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
namespace MyNamespace; // File-scoped namespace

public class Person(string name) { // Primary Constructor
    public string Name { get; } = name;
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using primary constructors on mutable classes where parameters shadow properties, causing naming confusion.

questions.question: What are primary constructors?
questions.answer: A C# feature allowing class constructor parameters to be defined directly on the class header, scope-accessible throughout the class body.

questions.question: What are file-scoped namespaces?
questions.answer: A declaration ending with a semicolon (namespace X;) that applies to the entire file, reducing bracket indent level.

topics.title: Procedural vs Object-Oriented Programming
topics.html:
Procedural vs Object-Oriented Programming

Course: Object-Oriented Programming

Understand the shift from action-based programming (functions operating on data) to object-based programming (entities bundling state and behavior together).

💡 Key Concepts

  • Procedural Paradigm: Programs organized as sequential steps, functions, and global variables.
  • Object-Oriented Paradigm: Programs organized as objects containing fields (data) and methods (logic).
  • Maintainability: OOP limits the side effects of changing state by encapsulating data inside objects.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// Procedural approach
double balance = 100.0;
double Withdraw(double b, double a) => b - a;

// OOP approach
public class Account {
    private double balance = 100.0;
    public void Withdraw(double a) => balance -= a;
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Writing "Anemic Domain Models" (objects with only properties and no behavior), which is just procedural code using classes as data bags.

questions.question: What is the main difference between procedural and OOP paradigms?
questions.answer: Procedural code separates functions from data. OOP bundles data and functions into self-contained objects.

questions.question: What is an anemic domain model?
questions.answer: A model containing classes with state (properties) but no behavior (methods), separating data from logic.

topics.title: Classes and Objects
topics.html:
Classes and Objects

Course: Object-Oriented Programming

Classes are blueprints defining properties and behaviors. Objects are instances of these blueprints allocated in memory.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Class: The compile-time template or blueprint definition.
  • Object: The runtime instance created using the "new" keyword.
  • State & Behavior: State is stored in fields, and behavior is executed through methods.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public class Car {
    public string Model { get; set; } // State
    public void Drive() => Console.WriteLine("Driving!"); // Behavior
}

Car myCar = new Car() { Model = "Sedan" }; // Object instance

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Confusing the class definition with the object instance, or attempting to read instance members on a null object reference.

questions.question: What is the difference between a class and an object?
questions.answer: A class is a logical blueprint. An object is a physical instance of that blueprint allocated in memory.

questions.question: What is instantiation?
questions.answer: The process of creating an object instance in memory using a class constructor.

topics.title: The Four Pillars of OOP
topics.html:
The Four Pillars of OOP

Course: Object-Oriented Programming

Discover Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, and Polymorphism, and how they apply to domain design.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Encapsulation: Hiding internal state variables and exposing access through public methods.
  • Abstraction: Hiding complex implementation details and showing only the essential interfaces.
  • Inheritance: Reusing class structure from parents to child subclasses.
  • Polymorphism: Handling multiple types through a single base contract.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public abstract class PaymentProvider {
    public abstract void ProcessPayment(decimal amount);
}
public class StripeProvider : PaymentProvider {
    public override void ProcessPayment(decimal amount) => Console.WriteLine($"Stripe charged {amount}");
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Deep inheritance hierarchies that violate Liskov Substitution, coupling child classes tightly to base class implementations.

questions.question: How does polymorphism improve software flexibility?
questions.answer: It allows code to operate on abstract contracts, making it easy to swap implementations without modifying callers.

questions.question: What is encapsulation?
questions.answer: Bundling data and methods into a class and restricting direct access to object internals to protect state integrity.

topics.title: Encapsulation & Access Modifiers
topics.html:
Encapsulation & Access Modifiers

Course: Object-Oriented Programming

Expose class members selectively using access modifiers: private, protected, internal, public, and private protected.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Private: Restricts access to the defining class body only.
  • Protected: Allows access inside the class and its derived child classes.
  • Public & Internal: Public allows universal access. Internal limits access to the compilation assembly.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public class BankAccount {
    private decimal balance = 0; // Private backing field
    public decimal Balance => balance; // Read-only property
    public void Deposit(decimal amount) => balance += amount;
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Making all class fields public by default, which bypasses validation rules and breaks encapsulation.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the internal access modifier?
questions.answer: It limits class or member visibility to the containing assembly, preventing usage by external projects.

questions.question: Why is encapsulation critical for data validation?
questions.answer: By restricting direct access to fields, it forces callers to go through properties or methods that validate inputs.

topics.title: Inheritance & Polymorphism
topics.html:
Inheritance & Polymorphism

Course: Object-Oriented Programming

Establish IS-A relationships and override base class behaviors to implement dynamic runtime dispatch.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Virtual & Override: Declaring methods as virtual in base classes to allow derived overrides.
  • Base Keyword: Invoking parent constructors or methods from within child classes.
  • Runtime Binding: The CLR determines which method to execute based on runtime object type.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public class Shape { public virtual void Draw() => Console.WriteLine("Drawing Shape"); }
public class Circle : Shape { public override void Draw() => Console.WriteLine("Drawing Circle"); }

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using inheritance for code sharing when there is no IS-A relationship, which creates fragile hierarchies.

questions.question: What is the difference between shadow (new) and override methods in C#?
questions.answer: override replaces the base method, preserving polymorphism. new hides the base method, disabling polymorphic dispatch.

questions.question: How is runtime polymorphism resolved?
questions.answer: The runtime looks at the actual object type on the heap (vtable lookup) rather than the variable reference type.

topics.title: Method Overloading vs Method Overriding
topics.html:
Method Overloading vs Method Overriding

Course: Object-Oriented Programming

Differentiate between static polymorphism (compile-time overloading) and dynamic polymorphism (runtime overriding).

💡 Key Concepts

  • Overloading: Multiple methods in a class with the same name but different signatures.
  • Overriding: Replacing a parent class virtual method with a custom subclass version.
  • Compile-time vs Runtime: Overloads are selected by the compiler; overrides are resolved at runtime.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public class Calculator {
    public int Add(int a, int b) => a + b; // Overload 1
    public double Add(double a, double b) => a + b; // Overload 2
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Creating overloads with ambiguous parameter signatures, causing compiler errors.

questions.question: Is method overloading determined at runtime?
questions.answer: No, method overloading is resolved at compile-time by matching the argument list to available signatures.

questions.question: Can you override static methods in C#?
questions.answer: No, static methods belong to the class itself, not to instances, and cannot be marked as virtual or overridden.

topics.title: Abstract Classes vs Interfaces
topics.html:
Abstract Classes vs Interfaces

Course: Object-Oriented Programming

Choose between abstract classes (providing shared state and base features) and interfaces (defining behavior contracts).

💡 Key Concepts

  • Abstract Class: A partial class blueprint that can define constructors and state fields.
  • Interface: A contract that can be implemented by any class or struct.
  • Multiple Inheritance: C# allows implementing multiple interfaces but only inheriting from one class.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public interface IFlyable { void Fly(); }
public abstract class Bird { public abstract void Eat(); }

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using an abstract class when an interface is needed, which limits subclass options due to C#'s single inheritance rule.

questions.question: When should you use an abstract class over an interface?
questions.answer: Use an abstract class when you want to provide shared code, constructors, or internal state (fields) to all subclasses.

questions.question: Can an interface have fields in C#?
questions.answer: No, interfaces cannot declare instance fields, though they can declare properties (which act as get/set method contracts).

topics.title: Composition vs Inheritance
topics.html:
Composition vs Inheritance

Course: Object-Oriented Programming

Favor composition over inheritance to create flexible, loosely coupled designs using HAS-A relationships.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Inheritance (IS-A): Tightly binds derived classes to base class code (compile-time).
  • Composition (HAS-A): Referencing helper classes inside an object, allowing runtime switches.
  • Loose Coupling: Composition makes classes easier to test by injecting mock dependencies.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public class Engine { public void Start() => Console.WriteLine("Vroom"); }
public class Car {
    private Engine engine = new Engine(); // Composition
    public void Drive() => engine.Start();
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Creating deep class hierarchies for code reuse, making the system fragile when base class code changes.

questions.question: Why is "favor composition over inheritance" a best practice?
questions.answer: Because composition creates loosely coupled systems where classes can change independently without breaking child class assumptions.

questions.question: What is a HAS-A relationship?
questions.answer: A design relationship where one class holds a reference to an instance of another class to delegate work.

topics.title: SOLID Principles
topics.html:
SOLID Principles

Course: Object-Oriented Programming

Learn the five core principles of object-oriented design to keep software maintainable, extensible, and clean.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Single Responsibility: A class should have only one reason to change.
  • Open/Closed: Classes should be open for extension but closed for modification.
  • Liskov Substitution: Subclasses must be substitutable for their parent classes without errors.
  • Interface Segregation: Prefer small, focused interfaces over large, general-purpose ones.
  • Dependency Inversion: High-level modules should depend on interfaces, not concrete implementations.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public interface IRepository { void Save(); }
public class SqlRepository : IRepository { public void Save() { /* Sql logic */ } }
public class Controller {
    private IRepository repo;
    public Controller(IRepository r) => repo = r; // Inversion of Dependency
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Writing monolithic classes that handle database access, validation, and email notification, violating the Single Responsibility Principle.

questions.question: How does Dependency Inversion relate to Dependency Injection?
questions.answer: Dependency Inversion is the design goal (coding to interfaces). Dependency Injection is the mechanism used to pass dependencies at runtime.

questions.question: What does the Open/Closed Principle solve?
questions.answer: It prevents introducing bugs into working production code by adding features via subclasses or interfaces instead of modifying existing classes.

topics.title: GRASP Patterns
topics.html:
GRASP Patterns

Course: Object-Oriented Programming

General Responsibility Assignment Software Patterns (GRASP) outline object design and class responsibility assignment guidelines.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Information Expert: Assign responsibility to the class that holds the required information.
  • Creator: Assign class B responsibility to create class A if B aggregates or uses A closely.
  • Controller: First object beyond the UI that coordinates system operations.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// Information Expert Example
public class OrderItem { public decimal Price; public int Qty; }
public class Order {
    private List<OrderItem> items;
    public decimal GetTotal() => items.Sum(i => i.Price * i.Qty); // Information Expert
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Assigning calculation logic to a controller instead of the object that owns the data, violating the Information Expert pattern.

questions.question: What is the Information Expert pattern?
questions.answer: A principle stating that responsibility should be assigned to the information expert—the object that has the information necessary to fulfill the responsibility.

questions.question: What is the Creator pattern in GRASP?
questions.answer: It guides deciding which object should create a new instance of a class based on ownership and reference relationships.

topics.title: Coupling & Cohesion
topics.html:
Coupling & Cohesion

Course: Object-Oriented Programming

Aim for high cohesion (focused class responsibility) and loose coupling (minimized class dependencies).

💡 Key Concepts

  • High Cohesion: A class does one job and does it completely, keeping logic focused.
  • Loose Coupling: Minimizing relationships between classes so changes are isolated.
  • Refactoring benefits: Cohesive and loosely coupled systems are easier to test and modify.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// High Cohesion: Focused purely on parsing JSON
public class JsonParser {
    public T Parse<T>(string data) => JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>(data);
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Creating "God Classes" (low cohesion) that manage many unrelated tasks, making the codebase fragile.

questions.question: What is the difference between coupling and cohesion?
questions.answer: Cohesion refers to how focused a class's responsibilities are. Coupling refers to how dependent classes are on each other.

questions.question: Why is high coupling bad?
questions.answer: Because a change in one class forces changes across many other classes, creating a fragile system.

topics.title: Association, Aggregation, and Composition
topics.html:
Association, Aggregation, and Composition

Course: Object-Oriented Programming

Understand the differences between object relationships: Association (using), Aggregation (has a), and Composition (owns a).

💡 Key Concepts

  • Association: A general relationship where objects use each other (doctor and patient).
  • Aggregation: A weak relationship where child objects can survive without the parent (car and wheel).
  • Composition: A strong relationship where child objects cannot exist without the parent (house and room).

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// Composition: Room dies if House is destroyed
public class House {
    private List<Room> rooms = new List<Room>();
}
// Aggregation: Wheel survives if Car is destroyed
public class Car {
    private List<Wheel> wheels;
    public Car(List<Wheel> w) => wheels = w;
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Implementing relationships as Composition when they should be Aggregation, which deletes child data prematurely.

questions.question: What is the difference between Aggregation and Composition?
questions.answer: In composition, child lifetimes are controlled by the parent. In aggregation, child objects can exist independently of the parent.

questions.question: What is an Association relationship?
questions.answer: A loose relationship where two independent classes interact without owning each other.

topics.title: Design for Testability
topics.html:
Design for Testability

Course: Object-Oriented Programming

Write testable code by avoiding static classes, using dependency injection, and coding to interface abstractions.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Inversion of Control: Letting external frameworks manage object dependencies.
  • Mocking abstractions: Creating dummy service classes to test units in isolation.
  • Avoiding global state: Avoiding singletons and static fields that make test isolation difficult.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
public interface IClock { DateTime Now { get; } }
public class OrderService {
    private IClock clock;
    public OrderService(IClock c) => clock = c;
    public bool IsExpired(Order o) => clock.Now > o.ExpiryDate; // Testable!
}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Instantiating external services directly (e.g. new EmailService()) inside method bodies, which makes unit testing impossible without sending real emails.

questions.question: Why does coding to interfaces improve unit testing?
questions.answer: It allows swapping real dependencies (like databases or APIs) with mock classes during test execution.

questions.question: How does global static state affect unit test isolation?
questions.answer: Static state is shared across tests, meaning one test can modify values and cause subsequent tests to fail unexpectedly.

topics.title: Code Smells & Refactoring
topics.html:
Code Smells & Refactoring

Course: Object-Oriented Programming

Identify code smells like long methods, duplicate code, and feature envy, and apply patterns to fix them.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Long Parameter List: Fix by grouping related parameters into parameter objects.
  • Feature Envy: A method that uses data from another class more than its own. Move the method.
  • Refactoring definition: Improving internal code structure without changing external behavior.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// Before: Long parameter list
public void CreateUser(string name, string street, string city, string zip) { }
// After: Parameter Object
public record Address(string Street, string City, string Zip);
public void CreateUser(string name, Address addr) { }

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Adding features while refactoring, which makes debugging difficult if tests fail.

questions.question: What is Feature Envy?
questions.answer: A code smell where a method in class A accesses variables of class B repeatedly. Fix it by moving the method into class B.

questions.question: What is the goal of refactoring?
questions.answer: To clean up code structure, improve readability, and reduce complexity without changing how the program behaves outwardly.

topics.title: Monolithic vs Microservices Architecture
topics.html:
Monolithic vs Microservices Architecture

Course: Microservices

Compare building a single combined application (Monolithic) with distributing features across independent, modular services (Microservices).

💡 Key Concepts

  • Monolith: All modules are built, deployed, and scaled together in a single code base.
  • Microservices: Autonomous services organized around business capabilities, with their own databases.
  • Independent Deployment: Services can be updated individually without redeploying the whole system.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// Monolith: Shared in-memory service calls
var data = orderService.GetOrderDetails(id);

// Microservices: HTTP or gRPC cross-network call
var data = await httpClient.GetFromJsonAsync<Order>($"http://order-service/api/orders/{id}");

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Adopting microservices too early for simple projects. The operational complexity of service discovery, networks, and logging can outweigh the benefits.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of microservices over a monolith?
questions.answer: Independent deployability, allowing teams to develop, scale, and deploy services without affecting the rest of the application.

questions.question: What is a distributed monolith?
questions.answer: An anti-pattern where services are separated but tightly coupled through synchronous calls, failing to achieve independent deployment.

topics.title: Characteristics of Microservices
topics.html:
Characteristics of Microservices

Course: Microservices

Review the defining features of microservices, including domain-driven design, smart endpoints, and database-per-service.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Domain-Driven Design: Services align with distinct business boundaries.
  • Database-per-Service: Each service owns its own database, preventing shared schema dependencies.
  • Smart endpoints, dumb pipes: Services process business logic; the network pipes only route messages.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// OrderService DB: OrderTables, OrderItems (SQL Server)
// CatalogService DB: ProductCatalog, Categories (MongoDB)

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Sharing a database database instance between two microservices, which creates schema coupling and invalidates service autonomy.

questions.question: Why is "Database-per-Service" a rule in microservices?
questions.answer: To ensure data isolation, allowing each service to use its own database type and evolve its schema independently without breaking other services.

questions.question: What does "smart endpoints, dumb pipes" mean?
questions.answer: The routing network (like RabbitMQ or HTTP) is simple and does not contain business logic; all logic lives inside the services.

topics.title: DDD, Bounded Contexts & Ubiquitous Language
topics.html:
DDD, Bounded Contexts & Ubiquitous Language

Course: Microservices

Use Domain-Driven Design (DDD) to identify bounded contexts and ubiquitous languages to guide microservice boundaries.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Bounded Context: A boundary within which a domain model is defined and valid.
  • Ubiquitous Language: A shared vocabulary used by both developers and business experts to define domain models.
  • Context Mapping: Defining how different bounded contexts interact and share data.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// Bounded Context: Ordering
public class Customer { public int Id; public List<Order> Orders; }

// Bounded Context: Identity
public class User { public int Id; public string PasswordHash; }

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Creating a single unified "User" or "Customer" model shared across all microservices, which couples different business areas.

questions.question: What is a Bounded Context?
questions.answer: A boundary within which a specific domain model applies, clarifying model terminology (e.g. User vs Customer).

questions.question: Why is a Ubiquitous Language important?
questions.answer: It aligns technical code models with business terminology, reducing translation errors and communication gaps.

topics.title: Database-per-Service vs Shared Database
topics.html:
Database-per-Service vs Shared Database

Course: Microservices

Contrast database encapsulation with shared schema patterns, and analyze schema coupling.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Encapsulation: Services expose data only through APIs, never through direct database access.
  • Polyglot Persistence: Choosing the best database type (SQL, NoSQL, graph) for each service.
  • Data replication: Duplicating lookup data to reduce cross-service queries.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// OrderService queries Customer details from CustomerService via API
// instead of query JOIN Customer database tables directly.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Writing SQL Joins across databases of different services, which violates encapsulation and breaks boundaries.

questions.question: What is Polyglot Persistence?
questions.answer: The practice of using multiple database storage technologies within an application based on service needs.

questions.question: How do you handle reporting across database-per-service architectures?
questions.answer: By streaming database changes (CDC) or events to a centralized Data Lake or Data Warehouse.

topics.title: Sync (gRPC/HTTP) vs Async (Event-Driven/Kafka)
topics.html:
Sync (gRPC/HTTP) vs Async (Event-Driven/Kafka)

Course: Microservices

Compare synchronous communication (blocking HTTP/gRPC calls) with asynchronous event-driven messaging (RabbitMQ/Kafka).

💡 Key Concepts

  • Synchronous (gRPC/HTTP): Direct request-response calls. Easiest to write, but blocks threads and creates runtime dependency.
  • Asynchronous (Events): Services publish event messages to a broker; subscribers react independently. Non-blocking.
  • gRPC benefits: Uses HTTP/2 and protocol buffers for fast, compact binary communication.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// Publishing an integration event to RabbitMQ
var orderEvent = new OrderCreatedEvent(order.Id);
await eventBus.PublishAsync(orderEvent);

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Chaining synchronous HTTP calls (A calls B, B calls C, C calls D), which amplifies latency and introduces multiple points of failure.

questions.question: Why is asynchronous communication preferred in microservices?
questions.answer: It decouples services, preventing a failure in one service from crashing the caller, and improves performance.

questions.question: When is gRPC preferred over REST/JSON?
questions.answer: For service-to-service internal communication where low latency, high throughput, and strong API contracts are needed.

topics.title: API Gateway & BFF (Backend for Frontend)
topics.html:
API Gateway & BFF (Backend for Frontend)

Course: Microservices

Implement API Gateways to route requests, manage security, and create custom backends for specific frontend client types.

💡 Key Concepts

  • API Gateway: A proxy server acting as the single entry point, routing requests to target microservices.
  • BFF Pattern: Creating separate gateway backends for different clients (e.g. mobile app vs web app).
  • Cross-cutting concerns: Offloading SSL handshakes, rate limiting, and authorization to the gateway.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// Web BFF routes to: OrderService /api/orders
// Mobile BFF routes to: OrderService /api/m/orders (with smaller payload)

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Adding complex business logic inside the API Gateway, converting it into a monolithic bottleneck.

questions.question: What is the Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern?
questions.answer: A pattern where you create separate API Gateways tailored to the specific needs of different client applications (web, mobile).

questions.question: Name three concerns offloaded to an API Gateway.
questions.answer: SSL termination, authentication/authorization, and rate limiting/throttling.

topics.title: Service Discovery & Dynamic Registries
topics.html:
Service Discovery & Dynamic Registries

Course: Microservices

Solve service address routing challenges in dynamic cloud environments using Service Registry and Discovery.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Service Registry: A database of active service instance IPs and ports.
  • Dynamic Registration: Instances register their addresses on startup and send health checks.
  • Client-side discovery: The client queries the registry to resolve service addresses.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// Consul Service Registration config in C#
var consulClient = new ConsulClient(c => c.Address = new Uri("http://consul:8500"));
await consulClient.Agent.ServiceRegister(registration);

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Not configuring container health checks in the registry, leading to traffic being routed to crashed containers.

questions.question: What is Service Discovery?
questions.answer: A mechanism that allows services to automatically detect and connect to other service instances in a dynamic environment.

questions.question: What is the role of Consul or Eureka?
questions.answer: They act as centralized service registries where instances register on startup and verify health.

topics.title: Distributed Transactions & Saga Pattern
topics.html:
Distributed Transactions & Saga Pattern

Course: Microservices

Maintain data consistency across multiple databases without 2PC (Two-Phase Commit) using the Saga Pattern.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Saga Pattern: A sequence of local transactions across services. Each step publishes an event.
  • Compensating Transaction: Undo actions executed to roll back database changes if a subsequent step fails.
  • Choreography vs Orchestration: Choreography is decentralized (event-based). Orchestration uses a central coordinator.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// Saga Orchestrator steps:
// 1. CreateOrderPending
// 2. AuthorizeCardPayment
// 3. (If payment fails) -> Rollback: CancelOrderPending (Compensating)

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Implementing Sagas without verifying that compensating steps are idempotent (can be run multiple times safely).

questions.question: What is a compensating transaction?
questions.answer: An action executed to undo the effects of a previous transaction step in a Saga if the workflow fails.

questions.question: What is the difference between Choreography and Orchestration in Sagas?
questions.answer: Choreography relies on services listening to events independently. Orchestration uses a central manager class to coordinate execution steps.

topics.title: CQRS & Event Sourcing Patterns
topics.html:
CQRS & Event Sourcing Patterns

Course: Microservices

Implement Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) and store application state as a sequence of events.

💡 Key Concepts

  • CQRS: Separates write models (Commands) from read models (Queries) to optimize performance.
  • Event Sourcing: Stores state changes as an immutable sequence of events instead of just the current record state.
  • Read Materialization: Replaying events to build read models in database caches.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// Event Sourcing model
var events = new List<Event> {
    new AccountCreatedEvent(id, 100),
    new MoneyDepositedEvent(id, 50),
    new MoneyWithdrawnEvent(id, 20)
}; // Current Balance (130) is rebuilt by replaying events

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Adopting Event Sourcing for simple domain models, which introduces high complexity for basic operations.

questions.question: What is CQRS?
questions.answer: Command Query Responsibility Segregation, a pattern that separates read and write operations into distinct database models.

questions.question: What is Event Sourcing?
questions.answer: Storing application state as a sequence of immutable events rather than overwriting database records.

topics.title: Fault Tolerance (Circuit Breakers, Bulkheads)
topics.html:
Fault Tolerance (Circuit Breakers, Bulkheads)

Course: Microservices

Prevent cascading failures across services using Retries, Timeout thresholds, Circuit Breakers, and Bulkheads.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Circuit Breaker: Trips open when a service fails repeatedly, preventing subsequent calls and failing fast.
  • Bulkhead Isolation: Limits resources (like threads) allocated to specific calls to prevent resource exhaustion.
  • Polly Library: A popular .NET library for implementing resilience patterns.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
var breakerPolicy = Policy
    .Handle<HttpRequestException>()
    .CircuitBreakerAsync(exceptionsAllowedBeforeBreaking: 3, durationOfBreak: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Configuring infinite retry policies without backing off, which creates a denial of service (DoS) effect on failing databases.

questions.question: What are the three states of a Circuit Breaker?
questions.answer: Closed (traffic flows), Open (calls fail instantly), and Half-Open (sends trial requests to check recovery).

questions.question: What is a Bulkhead pattern?
questions.answer: An isolation pattern that limits maximum thread pool or resource usage for specific service paths to prevent total system freeze.

topics.title: Centralized Logs & Observability
topics.html:
Centralized Logs & Observability

Course: Microservices

Track user requests across distributed services using Correlation IDs, centralized logs, and distributed tracing.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Correlation ID: A unique ID passed in HTTP headers to trace requests across services.
  • Distributed Tracing: Measuring execution latency across multiple services (Jaeger, OpenTelemetry).
  • Centralized Logging: Streaming log outputs from all containers to a single searchable dashboard (ELK).

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// Setting correlation ID header in C# HTTP client
client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Add("X-Correlation-ID", correlationId);

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Not logging Correlation IDs, which makes debugging requests across multiple services impossible.

questions.question: What is a Correlation ID?
questions.answer: A unique identifier passed between microservice calls to link logs from different systems to a single user action.

questions.question: What is OpenTelemetry?
questions.answer: An open-source standard for generating, collecting, and exporting logs, metrics, and traces from distributed apps.

topics.title: Containers and Kubernetes Orchestration
topics.html:
Containers and Kubernetes Orchestration

Course: Microservices

Understand how Docker and Kubernetes are used to package, deploy, and scale microservices.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Containerization: Bundling each microservice into a Docker image.
  • Kubernetes Pods: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes, containing one or more containers.
  • Declarative Scaling: Defining replica counts in YAML files to scale instances automatically.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// Kubernetes deployment yaml snippet
# spec:
#   replicas: 3
#   template:
#     spec:
#       containers:
#       - name: order-service

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Treating Kubernetes pods as permanent servers, forgetting that pods are temporary and can be destroyed at any time.

questions.question: What is a Kubernetes Pod?
questions.answer: The basic execution unit in Kubernetes, grouping containers that share storage and network settings.

questions.question: Why is container orchestration necessary for microservices?
questions.answer: To automate deployment, load balancing, scaling, health monitoring, and networking across multiple service instances.

topics.title: Microservices CI/CD Pipelines
topics.html:
Microservices CI/CD Pipelines

Course: Microservices

Build, test, and deploy microservices independently using CI/CD pipelines.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Continuous Integration: Automating code builds and testing on every pull request.
  • Continuous Deployment: Automatically deploying passing builds to staging or production.
  • Blue-Green Deployment: Deploying updates to a duplicate environment and switching traffic to prevent downtime.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// GitHub Actions workflow snippet
# - name: Build and Push Docker Image
#   run: |
#     docker build -t myacr.azurecr.io/orderservice:${{ github.sha }} .
#     docker push myacr.azurecr.io/orderservice:${{ github.sha }}

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Building a single monolithic deployment pipeline that builds all microservices on every change, instead of pipeline isolation.

questions.question: Why should microservices have separate CI/CD pipelines?
questions.answer: To allow each service to be built, tested, and deployed independently without affecting other services.

questions.question: What is Canary Deployment?
questions.answer: A release strategy where updates are deployed to a small percentage of users first to check stability before full rollout.

topics.title: Gateway Security (OAuth2, OIDC)
topics.html:
Gateway Security (OAuth2, OIDC)

Course: Microservices

Secure microservices using OAuth2 token verification and OpenID Connect (OIDC) protocols.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Token Verification: Microservices validate incoming JWT signatures using public keys.
  • Identity Provider (IdP): Central service (Keycloak, Auth0) that handles authentication and issues tokens.
  • Scope checking: Verifying token claims (e.g. read:orders) inside API controllers.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
[Authorize(Policy = "RequireReadScope")]
[HttpGet("{id}")]
public IActionResult GetOrder(int id) => Ok();

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Validating JWT signatures by calling the Identity Provider database on every microservice request, which hurts performance.

questions.question: How do microservices validate JWT tokens without contacting the Auth server?
questions.answer: They validate tokens in memory by checking the signature against the Auth server's public key (using JWKS).

questions.question: What is the role of an Identity Provider (IdP)?
questions.answer: A central service that authenticates users and issues tokens containing identity claims.

topics.title: Virtualization vs Containerization
topics.html:
Virtualization vs Containerization

Course: Docker & Containers

Understand the difference between virtualizing physical hardware (Virtual Machines) and isolating applications using the host OS kernel (Docker).

💡 Key Concepts

  • Hypervisor: Virtualizes hardware, requiring a complete guest OS for each VM.
  • Docker Engine: Containers share the host OS kernel, running as isolated processes.
  • Resource overhead: VMs use gigabytes of memory and take minutes to boot; containers start in seconds.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
Virtual Machine: [Hardware] -> [Hypervisor] -> [Guest OS] -> [App]
Docker Container: [Hardware] -> [Host OS] -> [Docker Engine] -> [App]

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Treating Docker containers like Virtual Machines by keeping them running permanently and editing files directly inside them.

questions.question: Why are containers more lightweight than VMs?
questions.answer: Because containers share the host operating system kernel instead of booting a complete guest OS.

questions.question: What is the role of the Docker daemon?
questions.answer: It manages Docker images, containers, networks, and storage volumes on the host system.

topics.title: Docker Engine Architecture
topics.html:
Docker Engine Architecture

Course: Docker & Containers

Explore the internal components of the Docker Engine: Daemon, REST API, Client, and registries.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Docker Client (CLI): The command-line interface used to send commands to the daemon.
  • Docker Daemon (dockerd): The background process that builds, runs, and manages containers.
  • Containerd: The low-level container runtime that manages container lifecycles.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
Client (docker run) ──(REST API)──> Daemon (dockerd) ──> containerd ──> runc ──> Container

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Running the Docker daemon without security access limits, which can expose root access on the host system.

questions.question: What is dockerd?
questions.answer: The background daemon process that manages container lifecycles, images, networks, and storage.

questions.question: What is containerd?
questions.answer: An industry-standard container runtime used by Docker to manage container execution.

topics.title: Installation & Configuration
topics.html:
Installation & Configuration

Course: Docker & Containers

Configure Docker Desktop, allocate CPU/RAM limits, and configure proxy connections.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Docker Desktop: GUI application providing container runtimes on Windows and macOS.
  • WSL 2 Backend: Integrates Docker on Windows using Windows Subsystem for Linux.
  • Resource Limits: Setting CPU, memory, and swap space allocations for container execution.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
# Allocating memory limits in docker-compose or run commands
docker run -m 512m --cpus="1.5" nginx

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Not setting container memory limits, allowing a memory leak in a container to exhaust host RAM and crash the host OS.

questions.question: Why is WSL 2 preferred for Docker on Windows?
questions.answer: It provides faster compilation, performance, and compatibility compared to older Hyper-V architectures.

questions.question: How do you check current resource allocations in Docker?
questions.answer: By executing "docker info" or using Docker Desktop settings.

topics.title: CLI Essentials (run, build, exec, logs)
topics.html:
CLI Essentials (run, build, exec, logs)

Course: Docker & Containers

Master the core Docker commands to build images, run containers, inspect logs, and execute terminal commands.

💡 Key Concepts

  • docker build: Compiles a Dockerfile into an executable container image.
  • docker run: Instantiates and runs a container from an image, mapping ports.
  • docker exec: Runs a terminal command inside an already running container.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
docker build -t my-web-app .
docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web my-web-app
docker exec -it web sh
docker logs web

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using docker run repeatedly to restart stopped containers, which creates duplicate container instances instead of using docker start.

questions.question: What is the difference between docker run and docker start?
questions.answer: docker run creates and starts a new container instance. docker start boots an already existing stopped container.

questions.question: What does the -it flag do in docker exec?
questions.answer: It enables interactive mode and allocates a pseudo-TTY terminal, allowing you to interact with the container shell.

topics.title: Images, Layers & Cache
topics.html:
Images, Layers & Cache

Course: Docker & Containers

Understand Docker image layer caching and write instructions that utilize caching for faster builds.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Read-Only Layers: Images consist of stacked, read-only filesystem layers.
  • Build Cache: Docker reuse unchanged layers to speed up compilation.
  • Union File System: Combines all layers into a single cohesive file system view.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
# Each line in a Dockerfile creates a new layer
# Placing frequently changed lines (COPY source) at the bottom
# allows cached dependency restores (RUN dotnet restore) to remain valid.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Changing files that are copied early in the Dockerfile, which invalidates the cache for all subsequent steps and slows down builds.

questions.question: How does Docker build caching work?
questions.answer: Docker checks if the instructions and files in a step match previous builds; if so, it reuses the cached layer instead of running the command again.

questions.question: What happens to layers when you modify a Dockerfile line?
questions.answer: The cache for that modified line and all subsequent lines is invalidated, forcing those steps to rebuild.

topics.title: Writing a Dockerfile
topics.html:
Writing a Dockerfile

Course: Docker & Containers

Learn the core instructions to write clean Dockerfiles: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, EXPOSE, CMD, and ENTRYPOINT.

💡 Key Concepts

  • FROM / WORKDIR: Selects the base image and configures the working directory.
  • RUN vs CMD: RUN executes commands at build time. CMD defines default runtime commands.
  • ENTRYPOINT: Defines the main executable binary file run when the container starts.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0
WORKDIR /app
COPY ./publish .
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "MyAPI.dll"]

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using RUN to start applications, not understanding that RUN commands run only at compile time and are baked into the image.

questions.question: What is the difference between RUN and CMD?
questions.answer: RUN runs commands during image build (creating layers). CMD defines the default command executed when the container starts.

questions.question: How do CMD and ENTRYPOINT interact?
questions.answer: ENTRYPOINT defines the executable. CMD acts as default arguments passed to that executable.

topics.title: Multi-Stage Build Configurations
topics.html:
Multi-Stage Build Configurations

Course: Docker & Containers

Create small production images by separating build-time SDK packages from runtime environments.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Build-time dependencies: Using full compilers (like .NET SDK or npm) to compile code in a temporary stage.
  • Runtime base images: Deploying compiled output to lightweight runtime images (like Alpine or aspnet-runtime).
  • COPY --from: Copying compiled files between build stages.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:8.0 AS build-stage
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN dotnet publish -c Release -o /app/out

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build-stage /app/out .

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Including SDK layers in production images, resulting in large image sizes and security vulnerabilities.

questions.question: Why are multi-stage builds recommended for production?
questions.answer: They reduce the final image size and improve security by omitting build tools, compilers, and source code.

questions.question: What does the AS keyword do in FROM statements?
questions.answer: It assigns a name to a build stage, allowing it to be referenced in subsequent COPY --from commands.

topics.title: Volumes & Persistent Storage
topics.html:
Volumes & Persistent Storage

Course: Docker & Containers

Persist container data beyond container lifetimes using Named Volumes, Bind Mounts, and tmpfs.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Ephemerality: Container files are destroyed if the container is deleted.
  • Named Volumes: Storage areas managed by Docker on the host disk. Best for databases.
  • Bind Mounts: Mapping a specific folder from the host computer into a container.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
docker run -d -p 5432:5432 -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres
# Maps named volume pgdata to postgres data directory

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Storing database records inside the container filesystem without mounting a volume, resulting in total data loss when the container is deleted.

questions.question: What is the difference between a volume and a bind mount?
questions.answer: Volumes are managed by Docker. Bind mounts link to a specific path on the host system.

questions.question: What happens to volume data when a container is deleted?
questions.answer: The volume data is preserved; it remains on the host disk and can be mounted to another container.

topics.title: Docker Networking Modes
topics.html:
Docker Networking Modes

Course: Docker & Containers

Configure communication between containers using networking modes: Bridge, Host, Overlay, and None.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Bridge Network: The default network. Containers communicate using container names as DNS names.
  • Host Network: Bypasses network isolation, mapping container ports directly to host ports.
  • Overlay Network: Enables communication between containers on different host computers (Swarm/K8s).

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
docker network create my-bridge
docker run -d --name db --network my-bridge postgres
docker run -d --name web --network my-bridge -p 80:80 my-web-app

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Attempting to make containers talk to each other using "localhost" instead of container names inside a custom network.

questions.question: How do containers resolve each other's IP addresses on a custom bridge network?
questions.answer: Docker provides a built-in DNS service that resolves container names to their internal IPs.

questions.question: What is the default network mode for Docker containers?
questions.answer: The default network mode is Bridge.

topics.title: Docker Compose Multi-Container Orchestration
topics.html:
Docker Compose Multi-Container Orchestration

Course: Docker & Containers

Define and run multi-container applications (e.g. API + Database + Redis) using a single docker-compose.yml file.

💡 Key Concepts

  • docker-compose.yml: Declarative YAML file defining services, networks, and volumes.
  • Service dependencies: Configuring start order using the depends_on attribute.
  • CLI management: Managing the entire application stack using "docker-compose up -d".

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
version: "3.8"
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "5000:80"
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Assuming depends_on waits for the database to be fully initialized and ready. It only waits for the database container process to start. You must implement retry logic in your application.

questions.question: What is Docker Compose?
questions.answer: A tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications using a single YAML configuration file.

questions.question: How do you stop and remove all resources created by Docker Compose?
questions.answer: By executing the "docker-compose down" command in the directory containing the compose file.

topics.title: Resource Limits & Container Monitoring
topics.html:
Resource Limits & Container Monitoring

Course: Docker & Containers

Monitor container performance, CPU utilization, and allocate runtime memory limits.

💡 Key Concepts

  • docker stats: CLI tool displaying real-time CPU, memory, network, and disk usage metrics.
  • Memory Limits: Restricting container RAM to prevent resource exhaustion.
  • CPU Pinning: Allocating specific CPU cores to high-priority containers.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
docker stats --no-stream # Returns instant container resource snapshot

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Not monitoring container metrics in production, leaving memory leaks or deadlocked threads undetected.

questions.question: How do you check resource usage stats of running containers?
questions.answer: By executing the "docker stats" command in the terminal.

questions.question: What happens if a container exceeds its configured memory limit?
questions.answer: The host system will terminate the container process using the Out Of Memory (OOM) killer.

topics.title: Image Registries (Docker Hub, ECR, ACR)
topics.html:
Image Registries (Docker Hub, ECR, ACR)

Course: Docker & Containers

Publish, version, and pull container images from public and private registries.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Docker Registry: A storage and hosting service for Docker images.
  • Image Tagging: Naming and versioning images (e.g. myimage:v1.2).
  • Private Registries: Authenticating with private cloud registries (AWS ECR, Azure ACR, GitHub Packages).

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
docker tag myapp:latest myusername/myapp:v1.0
docker push myusername/myapp:v1.0

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Pushing sensitive credentials (API keys, connection strings) inside pushed images, exposing them to anyone with image pull access.

questions.question: What is a Docker Registry?
questions.answer: A centralized service (like Docker Hub or Azure Container Registry) used to store and distribute Docker images.

questions.question: How do you version a Docker image during build?
questions.answer: By appending a tag to the image name (e.g., myapp:1.0.0) using the -t flag.

topics.title: Docker Security Policies
topics.html:
Docker Security Policies

Course: Docker & Containers

Secure Docker environments by running containers as non-root users and scanning images for vulnerabilities.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Non-Root execution: Using the USER directive in Dockerfiles to prevent host system exploits.
  • Image Scanning: Scanning images for security vulnerabilities in dependencies.
  • Read-only container rootfs: Running containers with read-only filesystems to prevent hackers from saving scripts.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
# Create non-root user in Dockerfile
RUN useradd -u 8888 appuser
USER appuser
# Container now executes safely as non-root user

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Running database or web containers with host root privileges, which allows hackers to escape the container and compromise the host.

questions.question: Why should you avoid running containers as root?
questions.answer: Because if a hacker breaches the container application, they gain root access to the underlying host system.

questions.question: What does the USER directive do in a Dockerfile?
questions.answer: It sets the username or UID to use when running subsequent image instructions and container runtime processes.

topics.title: Orchestration (Docker Swarm / Kubernetes Intro)
topics.html:
Orchestration (Docker Swarm / Kubernetes Intro)

Course: Docker & Containers

Introduction to orchestrating containers across clusters of host nodes using Swarm or Kubernetes.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Clustering: Grouping multiple virtual or physical machines into a single resource pool.
  • Declarative Scaling: Specifying the desired number of container replicas.
  • Rolling Updates: Updating container instances sequentially to prevent downtime.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
# Deploying a service stack to Docker Swarm
docker stack deploy -c docker-compose.yml myapp

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Designing stateful databases as replicas in clusters without configuring persistent distributed storage, leading to database synchronization errors.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a container orchestrator?
questions.answer: To manage deployment, scaling, load balancing, and networking of containers across a cluster of host machines.

questions.question: Name two popular container orchestrators.
questions.answer: Kubernetes and Docker Swarm.

topics.title: RDBMS Concepts & SQL Server Architecture
topics.html:
RDBMS Concepts & SQL Server Architecture

Course: SQL Server

Understand relational database concepts, primary/foreign key mappings, and the SQL Server storage engine.

💡 Key Concepts

  • RDBMS: Relational Database Management System based on tables, columns, and relations.
  • SQL Server Engine: The database engine coordinating memory allocation, indexing, and query tasks.
  • Schemas: Namespace containers used to group related tables and procedures (e.g. dbo, sales).

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
CREATE DATABASE TutorialDb;
GO
USE TutorialDb;
GO

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Treating a relational database as a flat file system, creating massive tables with duplicated columns instead of normal relations.

questions.question: What is an RDBMS?
questions.answer: A relational database management system that organizes data into tables and enforces relationships using keys.

questions.question: What does GO signify in SQL Server scripts?
questions.answer: It is a batch terminator utility command, telling SQL Server to execute previous statements together.

topics.title: Schema, Tables, Primary & Foreign Keys
topics.html:
Schema, Tables, Primary & Foreign Keys

Course: SQL Server

Establish database tables, enforce integrity constraints, and map relations using primary and foreign keys.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Primary Key: A column (or columns) that uniquely identifies each row in a table. Cannot be null.
  • Foreign Key: A column that establishes a link to the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity.
  • Constraints: Rules enforced on columns like NOT NULL, UNIQUE, and CHECK.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
CREATE TABLE Departments (
    Id INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY(1,1),
    Name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE Employees (
    Id INT PRIMARY KEY IDENTITY(1,1),
    Name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    DeptId INT FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Departments(Id)
);

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Not defining foreign keys and relying purely on application-level checks, which leads to orphaned records in the database.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a foreign key constraint?
questions.answer: To maintain referential integrity between tables by ensuring a value in one table matches an existing value in another.

questions.question: What does the IDENTITY(1,1) specification do?
questions.answer: It automatically generates unique auto-incrementing numbers for the column, starting at 1 and incrementing by 1.

topics.title: Querying Essentials (SELECT, GROUP BY, HAVING)
topics.html:
Querying Essentials (SELECT, GROUP BY, HAVING)

Course: SQL Server

Master writing queries: filter rows with WHERE, group data with GROUP BY, and apply group filters with HAVING.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Logical Query Order: SQL parses clauses in this order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY.
  • GROUP BY: Groups rows sharing key values to run aggregate functions (SUM, COUNT, AVG).
  • HAVING vs WHERE: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
SELECT DeptId, COUNT(*) AS EmpCount
FROM Employees
WHERE IsActive = 1
GROUP BY DeptId
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5; // Group filter

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Attempting to filter aggregated columns in the WHERE clause, which causes compile errors because WHERE runs before grouping.

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
questions.answer: WHERE filters individual source rows before grouping. HAVING filters grouped/aggregated values after grouping.

questions.question: In what order does SQL Server process query clauses?
questions.answer: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY.

topics.title: SQL Joins (Inner, Left, Right, Full, Cross, Self)
topics.html:
SQL Joins (Inner, Left, Right, Full, Cross, Self)

Course: SQL Server

Combine data across related tables using standard join types.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Inner Join: Returns only the rows that have matching values in both tables.
  • Left / Right Join: Left Join returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right table, filling with nulls if there is no match.
  • Cross Join: Returns the Cartesian product of the two tables (every combination).

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
SELECT e.Name, d.Name AS DeptName
FROM Employees e
LEFT JOIN Departments d ON e.DeptId = d.Id;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Forgetting the join condition (the ON clause) in traditional joins, which generates huge Cartesian products and exhausts database memory.

questions.question: What happens during a Left Join if no match is found in the right table?
questions.answer: The query returns all columns for the right table as NULL values.

questions.question: What is a Self Join?
questions.answer: A join where a table is joined with itself (e.g. matching employees to their managers in the same table).

topics.title: Set Operations (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)
topics.html:
Set Operations (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)

Course: SQL Server

Combine query outputs using set algebra: UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT.

💡 Key Concepts

  • UNION: Combines outputs and filters out duplicate rows.
  • UNION ALL: Appends query results directly, retaining duplicates. Faster than UNION.
  • INTERSECT / EXCEPT: INTERSECT returns common rows. EXCEPT returns rows from query 1 not present in query 2.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
SELECT City FROM Customers
UNION ALL
SELECT City FROM Suppliers; // Retains duplicates

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using UNION instead of UNION ALL when you do not care about duplicate rows. UNION is slower because it performs a sort to remove duplicates.

questions.question: Why is UNION ALL faster than UNION?
questions.answer: Because UNION ALL appends the result sets immediately, while UNION must sort the combined set to filter out duplicates.

questions.question: What are the rules for combining queries with set operators?
questions.answer: Queries must have the same number of columns in the same order, with compatible data types.

topics.title: Built-in Scalar & Aggregate Functions
topics.html:
Built-in Scalar & Aggregate Functions

Course: SQL Server

Manipulate strings, calculate dates, and compute metrics using functions.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Scalar Functions: Operate on a single value and return a single value (SUBSTRING, GETDATE).
  • Aggregate Functions: Operate on a column of values and return a single summary (SUM, COUNT, AVG).
  • Coalesce: Returns the first non-null argument in a parameter list.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
SELECT Name, COALESCE(Phone, Email, 'No Contact') AS ContactInfo
FROM Customers;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Applying scalar functions to indexed columns in WHERE clauses, which prevents the query optimizer from performing Index Seeks.

questions.question: What is the COALESCE function used for?
questions.answer: It evaluates arguments sequentially and returns the first non-NULL value in the list.

questions.question: Name three common SQL Server aggregate functions.
questions.answer: COUNT(), SUM(), and AVG().

topics.title: Subqueries & CTEs (Common Table Expressions)
topics.html:
Subqueries & CTEs (Common Table Expressions)

Course: SQL Server

Simplify complex queries using nested subqueries, Correlated Subqueries, and Common Table Expressions (CTEs).

💡 Key Concepts

  • Subquery: A query nested inside another query (e.g. in the WHERE clause).
  • CTE (WITH): A temporary named result set defined within the execution scope of a single query.
  • Correlated Subquery: A nested query that references columns from the outer query, running once per row.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
WITH Sales_CTE AS (
    SELECT SalesPersonId, SUM(Amount) AS TotalSales
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY SalesPersonId
)
SELECT * FROM Sales_CTE WHERE TotalSales > 50000;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using deeply nested subqueries instead of CTEs, which makes SQL code hard to read and maintain.

questions.question: What is a Common Table Expression (CTE)?
questions.answer: A temporary named result set that can be referenced within a SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement.

questions.question: What is a correlated subquery?
questions.answer: A subquery that depends on columns from the outer query and is executed once for each row processed by the outer query.

topics.title: Stored Procedures & User Defined Functions
topics.html:
Stored Procedures & User Defined Functions

Course: SQL Server

Encapsulate SQL logic into reusable databases assets: Stored Procedures and User Defined Functions (UDFs).

💡 Key Concepts

  • Stored Procedure: Precompiled SQL code block. Can return multiple datasets, modify data, and take parameters.
  • User Defined Function (UDF): Calculates and returns a single scalar value or a table. Cannot modify data.
  • Execution Plan Caching: Procedures compile once and cache plans for faster subsequent executions.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
CREATE PROCEDURE GetEmployeeById @EmpId INT
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE Id = @EmpId;
END;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using scalar User Defined Functions inside SELECT lists on large tables, which causes SQL Server to execute the function row-by-row (RBAR - Row By Agonizing Row) and ruins performance.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a Stored Procedure and a Function?
questions.answer: Procedures can modify database tables and execute transactions. Functions cannot modify state and must return a value.

questions.question: What is parameter sniffing?
